A1.justification: Both PDFs describe M-DESIGN and retain matching methods, benchmarks, and results despite the title and organization changes. All 14 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including v2 Appendices A–C, support comparison through text extraction and visual inspection.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-selection experiments, ablations, efficiency measurements, and graph, tabular, and image benchmark results in Section V.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results in Section 5 and Appendix C, including benchmark comparisons, ablations, and refinement trajectories.

M1.justification: V1 uses predictive planners for OOD-flagged source tasks. V2 Section 4.3 additionally specifies substituting predictions for unrecorded modification edges, extending the stated prediction rule. The one-hop refinement loop, Bayesian similarity updates, sliding windows, EdgeConv planners, and replay-based adaptation remain. The new multi-hop terminology does not specify a separate multi-hop search algorithm.

E1.justification: The 22 graph datasets, 33 graph task-data pairs, four tabular datasets, and three image datasets are retained. V2 Section 5.4 newly mentions simulated missing repository edges, but does not identify a distinct experiment or connect that condition to separate results. Whether this establishes additional test-scenario coverage is unclear.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same baselines: ten for node classification and nine for link prediction and graph classification, with KBG absent from the latter two in both versions. The tabular MBMS comparator, described using GraphGym's ranking approach in v1, appears as GraphG. in v2 with identical results; this does not establish a new comparator.

E3.justification: The shared model space, 100-evaluation budget, held-out target datasets, and efficiency target based on M-DESIGN's first 50 evaluations remain unchanged. V2's missing-edge simulation statement lacks an edge-removal procedure or an identified affected comparison, preventing a reliable distinction between a changed OOD protocol and additional description of existing tests.

E4.justification: V2 Figure 9 extends v1 Figure 10's convergence analysis from four to ten dataset cases, adding Actor, CiteSeer, Cora, DBLP, PubMed, and Texas. This broadens evidence about refinement trajectories within existing coverage. Component ablations, assumption checks, local-consistency analyses, and initialization sensitivity results are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over ten trials and already display shaded trajectories. V2 Section 5.1 explicitly mentions different random seeds for stochastic baselines, and Appendix C.3 identifies shading as standard deviations over ten trials and explains unshaded retrieval curves. These are reporting clarifications, not evidence of increased run counts.

E6.justification: V2 Table 2 adds M-DESIGN's evaluations-to-target row, including 44 evaluations for Actor and 22 for Cornell. Figure 9 adds six dataset trajectory cases. Corresponding node, link, graph-classification, ablation, tabular, and image table values remain unchanged, as does the reported 26-of-33 optimum count.

T1.justification: V1 Theorem 1 asserts equivalence using an approximate probability-mixture argument. V2 Appendix B.1 replaces this central justification with conditioning on interaction history, an explicit Bayesian model-averaging assumption, and calibrated evidence incorporating gamma times the benchmark gain plus epsilon. This substantively revises the mathematical argument rather than merely relocating its proof.

C1.justification: The main adaptive-refinement contribution and numerical headline remain. V2's abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the planner claims to multi-hop extrapolation and reduced dependence on repository completeness, whereas v1 emphasizes predictive adaptation to OOD tasks and database-oriented refinement.

C2.justification: V2 explicitly identifies dynamic similarity as the primary driver and interprets OOD benefits through synthetic and multi-hop evidence. Section 6 adds limitations concerning repository coverage, local gain-model validity, extreme OOD tasks, and increased budget requirements. The impact statement also discusses inherited repository biases; these qualifications are absent from v1.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly states that test-set signals are excluded from retrieval and refinement. However, it omits v1's SQLite disclosure, planner L1 loss and Wasserstein evaluation details, the components excluded from the simplified tabular variant, and RGB-statistics initialization for images. Hardware, planner dimensions, and model-space documentation remain; these omissions do not establish implementation changes.

R1.justification: V2 substantially shifts positioning from a database-centric contribution toward retrieval-augmented automated model design. It adds work such as AutoML-Agent and Wasserstein task embedding, expands GNN and graph-NAS literature in Appendix A.3, and removes numerous database-oriented introductory citations. Retained model-base literature moves to Appendix A.2.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological narrative, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten around retrieval and edit-effect evidence. V2 introduces a dedicated related-work section, organizes experiments around five questions, and moves substantial background, methodology, and results into appendices. The title and contribution presentation also change.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the motivation and workflow illustrations, combines graph and pipeline concepts, restyles plots, and expands the supplementary trajectory display from eight to twenty panels. Numerous tables and the algorithm move to appendices. It also corrects the image-table dataset headings and the mislabeled Cora assumption-plot title.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful limitations, uncertainty-band explanations, corrected labels, and fuller efficiency and trajectory evidence. However, it removes reproducibility details and introduces multi-hop and missing-edge claims without a clearly specified corresponding evaluation. Appendix B.1's calibrated evidence also differs from Section 4.1's raw-or-predicted evidence definition. These competing gains and unresolved issues prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
